newsitem.title: JAPAN: Penalties loom for scandal-hit Nomura.
newsitem.headline: Penalties loom for scandal-hit Nomura.

text.p: Administrative penalties against top Japanese brokerage Nomura Securities loomed closer on Thursday after its president admitted it made illegal stock deals for a "sokaiya" corporate racketeer.
The admission by Nomura president Junichi Ujiie was made at a hearing held by Japan's Ministry of Finance (MOF) before it imposes penalties against Nomura.

"We will accept administrative penalties with solemnity," Ujiie replied when a MOF official told him that the ministry would impose penalties as it had confirmed through the hearing that Nomura violated Japan's Securities and Exchange Law.

Ujiie admitted allegations by the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission that Nomura provided racketeer Ryuichi Koike with about 47.5 million yen ($413,000) worth of benefits by transferring profits earned on its own dealings in 1995.
He said Nomura gave Koike about 2.2 million yen ($19,100) in benefits through illicit warrant transactions in March 1995.

He also admitted Nomura provided the racketeer with 320 million yen ($2.78 million) in cash in March 1995 but said the payment was made under off-balance sheet arrangements and it was difficult to clearly confirm how the cash was raised.
But he said former executives were involved in the cash payment and Nomura could not object to the allegation that the company itself provided funds from its assets to the racketeer.
"I deeply regret our activities, which ran contrary to fairness and transparency in the stock market," he said.
The ministry may order a brokerage violating the Securities and Exchange Law to suspend all or part of its operations for up to six months or to return its securities licences.
Financial analysts said penalties on Nomura -- mired in its second scandal in six years -- would be the heavier as it also violated the Commercial Code by making payoffs to a racketeer.
Some speculated it might face a partial suspension of its operations for four to five months.

Despite Ujiie's remarks at the hearing, however, shares in Nomura enjoyed heavy buying on the Tokyo Stock Exchange. It closed up 40 yen at 1,570 in trade of 6.22 million shares, the second-largest volume in the bourse's first section.

Traders said the stock market had largely digested the impact of the expected penalties since clients had already defected from the giant brokerage and it had also been suspended from underwriting government bonds.
The scandal was revealed in early March by Nomura itself.

Its shares hit the year's low of 1,100 yen on April 15, when fears mounted about the impact of the scandal on its future, but have recovered on perceptions that Nomura could maintain its top status in Japan's securities industry.
Thursday's gains also reflected speculation that punishment for its dealings with the racketeer would be lighter than earlier expected, traders said.

"There is speculation that only the department which has been directly involved with the racketeers and dealers trading on their own accounts will be punished, which would not be as bad as initially thought," said a foreign brokerage trader.

Another trader said: "Market participants think the punitive measures against Nomura have to be in line with those of Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank (DKB), which was also involved in the scandal... But the Ministry of Finance can't shut down its bank teller operations completely, which could mean that the Nomura punishment may not be very heavy."
Prosecutors have arrested more than 10 former DKB officials on suspicion of extending uncollateralised loans to Koike.

On Thursday, Japanese daily Mainichi Shimbun said prosecutors are likely to indict DKB for alleged violations of the banking law as early as next week if the MOF files a criminal complaint with prosecutors against the bank.
It said prosecutors are also likely to indict DKB's former chairman Tadashi Okuda on Friday on suspicion of illegally making bank loans to a racketeer. ($1=115 yen)
